items.prompt: What is 'validation,' as this unit defines it?
choices: Cheaply testing whether an assumption about what people want is actually true, before spending the effort to build the full solution
A formal legal review of a product before launch
Getting sign-off from a manager before starting a project
Running automated tests against a feature's code
items.explanation: Validation is specifically about cheaply testing an assumption before committing full build effort — not a legal, managerial, or automated-testing process.
items.reference:
Validation
💰 Cheap test
🎯 Of an assumption, before full build effort
Why: the point is confirming direction before spending the expensive effort.

items.prompt: In L1, what step did the team skip before building the six-week export feature?
choices: Validation of the underlying assumption that customers wanted a raw data export
Code review of the finished feature
A meeting with the sales team to discuss the request
Writing documentation for the new feature
items.explanation: The team built directly from an assumption relayed by sales, without any cheap test to confirm what customers actually wanted before committing six weeks of engineering.
items.reference:
Validation
💰 Cheap test
🎯 Of an assumption, before full build effort
Why: the point is confirming direction before spending the expensive effort.

items.prompt: What is a 'prototype,' as this unit defines it?
choices: A fast, low-effort stand-in for a feature, built specifically to test a question rather than to be shipped as the real thing
The final, polished version of a feature ready for release
A detailed technical specification document
A backup copy of a feature's source code
items.explanation: A prototype exists to answer a question cheaply — it's explicitly not meant to be the shipped, production version of the feature.
items.reference:
Prototype
⚡ Fast, low effort
❓ Built to test a question
Why: a prototype's job is answering a question, not being shippable.

items.prompt: In L3, what does the 'Export & Share' button actually do when clicked?

items.reference:
Prototype

items.prompt: What does this unit say an MVP (minimum viable product) actually is?
choices: The smallest version of an idea that can test the riskiest assumption behind it
The cheapest possible version of the final feature that still technically works
A product with the fewest possible bugs at launch
The first version of a product released to the public
items.explanation: L1 explicitly distinguishes an MVP from 'a smaller, cheaper version of the final feature' — its defining job is testing the riskiest assumption, not being a reduced version of the eventual product.
items.reference:
MVP
🎯 Tests the riskiest assumption
🚫 Not just 'smaller final feature'
Why: this distinction is the most common misreading of the term.

items.prompt: Would a version of the export feature with fewer file formats count as a true MVP, according to this unit?
choices: Not necessarily — it's still a smaller version of the same unconfirmed feature, not a test of whether customers want that feature at all
Yes — any smaller version of a feature automatically counts as an MVP
Yes, as long as it launches faster than the full version
No — an MVP must always be a non-functional mockup with zero real code
items.explanation: A feature with fewer formats is still committing engineering effort to the same unvalidated assumption — it's a smaller commitment, not a genuine test of the assumption itself.
items.reference:
MVP
🎯 Tests the riskiest assumption
🚫 Not just 'smaller final feature'
Why: this distinction is the most common misreading of the term.

items.prompt: What is the difference between an assumption and evidence, as this unit uses the terms?
choices: An assumption is a belief about what customers want; evidence is a real signal from actual behavior confirming or disproving it
An assumption is always false, while evidence is always true
There is no meaningful difference between the two terms
An assumption comes from customers directly; evidence always comes from competitors
items.explanation: The unit distinguishes belief (assumption) from confirmed, behavior-based signal (evidence) — assumptions aren't automatically wrong, they're just unconfirmed.
items.reference:
Assumption vs. evidence
💭 Assumption: unconfirmed belief
👁️ Evidence: real behavioral signal
Why: validation exists specifically to convert one into the other.

items.prompt: In L1, was 'sales says customers want to export their data' evidence or an assumption?

Evidence — sales talked directly to customers, so it counts as confirmed
Both equally, since the terms are interchangeable in this context
Neither — sales requests don't fall into either category
items.explanation: A secondhand report of what customers said they want is still an assumption until tested against real behavior — which is exactly what the team skipped.
items.reference:
Assumption vs. evidence
💭 Assumption: unconfirmed belief
👁️ Evidence: real behavioral signal
Why: validation exists specifically to convert one into the other.

🧪 Cheapest test
👁️ Real behavior observed
